title: What They Found Inside the Deepest Animals on Earth

scenes.text: A laboratory bench. A scientist opens the gut of an animal that has spent its entire life in permanent darkness, seven kilometres below the surface of the Pacific. Inside it is a blue fibre.
scenes.cap: It had never seen sunlight. It still had our clothing inside it.

scenes.text: Not on the seafloor beside it. Inside it. In the hindgut, where food goes.
The animal is an amphipod. A scavenger, about the size of your thumb, and the dominant scavenging animal in the deepest places on Earth.
scenes.cap: Amphipod. The deep sea's cleanup crew.

scenes.videoQuery: eyes on the seafloor geology ocean floor
scenes.text: In twenty nineteen, a team published what they found after examining ninety of them, pulled from six of the deepest trenches on the planet.

scenes.cap: Over 72% of individuals examined.
scenes.text: Over seventy two percent of the individuals examined contained at least one microparticle. Sixty five animals out of ninety.
scenes.stat: JAMIESON ET AL. · ROYAL SOCIETY OPEN SCIENCE · 2019 · doi:10.1098/rsos.180667

scenes.text: And in the deepest trench of all, the Mariana, the figure was not seventy two percent. It was one hundred.
Every single animal they brought up from the bottom of the world had something synthetic inside it.
scenes.cap: Every one.

scenes.text: This is the story of how we measured that, what else is down there with it, and the one question the measurements still cannot answer.

scenes.chapter:
WHAT THEY FOUND INSIDE
THE DEEPEST ANIMALS ON EARTH
scenes.text: What they found inside the deepest animals on Earth.
scenes.query: Mariana Trench bathymetry map Pacific seafloor NOAA public domain

scenes.chapter:
ACT I
THE ZONE THAT BEGINS AT SIX THOUSAND METRES

scenes.text: Oceanographers give the deepest water its own name. The hadal zone. It begins at six thousand metres and runs to just under eleven thousand.

scenes.videoQuery: geology ocean floor carbonate rocks flyover
scenes.text: It is not a layer that covers the ocean. It is a set of holes in it. Trenches, mostly around the rim of the Pacific, narrow and steep and separated from each other by thousands of kilometres of shallower water.
At the bottom of the deepest one, the water above you weighs down at more than a thousand times the pressure at the surface.
scenes.cap: Over 1,000 atmospheres.

scenes.text: You cannot simply go there. Almost everything we know about hadal animals comes from a machine that falls.
A baited lander is dropped over the side of a ship with weights attached. It free falls for hours. It sits on the bottom in the dark with a camera and a trap, and it waits.
Then it releases the weights and floats back up, and whatever came to the bait comes with it.
What comes to the bait, almost always, is amphipods. They arrive in their thousands. In the hadal zone they are the animals that clean up everything that dies above them.
Which makes them the perfect animal to test. Whatever is falling into the trench ends up passing through them.
scenes.cap: Everything that falls, they eat.

scenes.chapter:
ACT II
THE ANIMAL THAT GOT THERE FIRST

scenes.text: Before we get to what is in them, it is worth knowing what lives down there at all. Because the answer is stranger than empty.
This is the hadal snailfish. Pseudoliparis swirei. It lives between six and eight thousand metres, and it is the deepest vertebrate in the ocean.
scenes.cap: The deepest vertebrate known.
scenes.query: Pseudoliparis swirei hadal snailfish Mariana Trench NOAA specimen photograph

scenes.text: It has no scales. It is barely pigmented. It looks, honestly, like something unfinished.
And in twenty twenty three, a team sequenced its genome and found something nobody expected about how long it has been down there.

scenes.cap: Only in the last few million years.
scenes.text: The hadal snailfish, they wrote, may have entered and fully adapted to such extreme environments only in the last few million years.
A few million years. In evolutionary terms that is recent. And having got there, it spread into separate Pacific trenches within a million years more.

kinetic.sub: pigmentation · visual genes · skeletal calcification genes

scenes.text: Getting there cost it. The genome shows it lost its pigmentation. It lost visual genes. It lost genes for calcifying its own skeleton.

And it gained things. A compound called T M A O that stops proteins collapsing under pressure. And a duplicated gene for ferritin, which raised its tolerance to the reactive oxygen that would otherwise tear its cells apart.
For decades that was almost everything we knew. We had specimens. We did not have behaviour.
Then, this year, a team put a baited lander at nearly seven thousand metres, filmed what came, and tracked eight hundred and sixty eight separate sightings of individual fish.

kinetic.suffix: % of a body length per second
kinetic.sub: 0.16–0.18 m/s · the routine cruising speed of the deepest vertebrate on Earth

scenes.text: It moves slowly. About seven tenths of its own body length every second. A gentle, unhurried animal in the most hostile place there is.
And it finds food by smell. The same study estimated it first picks up the scent of bait from about three hundred and fifty metres away.
scenes.cap: It smells a meal from 350 metres.

scenes.text: That is the world we are talking about. Sparse, slow, patient, and until very recently, untouched by us in any way we could measure.

scenes.chapter:
ACT III
NINETY ANIMALS, SIX TRENCHES

scenes.text: The microplastics study is the one with the hardest numbers, so it is worth being precise about what it did.

scenes.cap: Japan · Izu-Bonin · Mariana · Kermadec · New Hebrides · Peru-Chile
scenes.text: Six trenches around the Pacific Rim. Japan. Izu Bonin. Mariana. Kermadec. New Hebrides. And Peru Chile. Depths from seven thousand metres to ten thousand eight hundred and ninety.
scenes.stat: JAMIESON ET AL. · ROYAL SOCIETY OPEN SCIENCE · 2019 · SIX TRENCHES, 7,000–10,890 m

scenes.text: From those six trenches, ninety amphipods. The researchers opened the hindgut of each one and looked for anything that was not food.
Over seventy two percent of them had at least one. Sixty five animals out of ninety.

I want to be careful with that number, because ninety animals is a small sample and the honest thing is to say so out loud. This is not a census of the deep ocean. It is ninety animals, from six places, examined one at a time.
But the pattern inside those ninety is very hard to look away from.

scenes.cap: 50% at the lowest. 100% at the deepest.
scenes.text: The frequency varied by site, between fifty percent and one hundred. The lowest was the New Hebrides Trench, at fifty percent. The highest was the Mariana, at one hundred percent.
scenes.stat: JAMIESON ET AL. · 2019 · FREQUENCY OF INGESTION BY SITE

scenes.text: The deepest trench on Earth had the highest contamination rate of all six. Not the one nearest a city. The deepest one.

kinetic.sub: fragments appeared in only 16% · fibres are the dominant form

scenes.text: Most of what they found was not fragments of hard plastic. It was fibre. Fibres appeared in eighty four percent of the animals. Fragments in only sixteen.

scenes.cap: Blue fibres. 66%.
scenes.text: And one item dominated. Blue fibres, in sixty six percent of all the animals. With, and I am quoting the paper, all amphipods sampled from the Mariana Trench containing at least one of these.
scenes.stat: JAMIESON ET AL. · 2019 · MOST PREVALENT ITEM INGESTED

scenes.text: A blue thread. In every animal, from the deepest place there is.

kinetic.sub: nylon · polyethylene · polyamide · polyvinyl alcohol · PVC · rayon · lyocell · ramie

scenes.text: They ran a subsample through infrared spectroscopy to find out what the fibres actually were. Nylon. Polyethylene. Polyamide. Polyvinyl alcohol. P V C, often with inorganic filler. Rayon and lyocell, which are semi synthetic. And ramie, which is a plant.

scenes.videoQuery: textile factory fabric weaving machine loom
scenes.text: That list is not a list of ocean things. It is a list of the things our clothes and our ropes and our packaging are made of.
scenes.cap: This is a list of our materials.

scenes.text: And then the paper makes the comparison that I think is the whole story.

scenes.cap: The same frequency as coastal crustaceans.
scenes.text: The animals in the hadal zone are ingesting plastic at, in the paper's words, a similar frequency, seventy two percent, to crustaceans in coastal water habitats.
Read that again. The deepest, most isolated animals on the planet are as likely to have plastic in them as the ones living just off our beaches.
scenes.cap: The bottom of the world is as contaminated as the shore.

scenes.chapter:
ACT IV
THE CHEMICALS THAT WERE SUPPOSED TO BE GONE

scenes.text: Two years before the plastics paper, the same lead researcher published something quieter and, I think, worse.
Not what the animals had swallowed. What had accumulated in their tissue.

Persistent organic pollutants. Industrial compounds built to not break down, which is exactly what makes them useful and exactly what makes them a problem. They do not degrade. They move up food chains and concentrate as they go.
scenes.cap: Built not to break down.
"Extraordinary levels."
scenes.text: Here we identify, they wrote, extraordinary levels of persistent organic pollutants in the endemic amphipod fauna from two of the deepest ocean trenches, over ten thousand metres.
scenes.stat: JAMIESON ET AL. · NATURE ECOLOGY & EVOLUTION · 2017 · doi:10.1038/s41559-016-0051

scenes.text: The two trenches were the Mariana and the Kermadec. Both over ten kilometres deep. Both thousands of kilometres from any heavy industry.

scenes.cap: Higher than regions of heavy industrialization.
scenes.text: And the sentence that matters. Contaminant levels were considerably higher than documented for nearby regions of heavy industrialization.
Higher in the trench than in the industrialised regions nearby. That is the finding. Not comparable. Higher.

I am going to be disciplined here, because this is where this story usually goes wrong. You will see a specific multiplier quoted for this study all over the internet. A number of times more contaminated than a named polluted river.

That figure is not in the paper's abstract, the full text sits behind a paywall, and the press release that carried it is gone. So we are not going to use it. What the authors published in the open is the sentence you just read, and it is more than enough.
scenes.cap: If we cannot source it, we do not say it.
Pervasive to full ocean depth.
scenes.text: Their conclusion was that this indicates bioaccumulation of anthropogenic contamination, and infers that these pollutants are pervasive across the world's oceans, and to full ocean depth.
The third measurement is not in the animals at all. It is in the mud they live on.
In twenty twenty one, a team took sediment cores from four trench regions, from fifteen hundred metres down to ten thousand eight hundred and forty, and measured the mercury in them.
Mercury is a neurotoxin, and like the organic pollutants, it concentrates as it moves up a food chain.

kinetic.sub: 24–220 µg per square metre per year · accumulating in the trenches

scenes.text: They found the trenches are accumulating mercury at between twenty four and two hundred and twenty micrograms per square metre per year. Greater than the global deep sea average, they wrote, by a factor of up to four hundred.

scenes.cap: Most of it comes from the surface.
scenes.text: And they traced where it came from. Most of the mercury in these trenches, they concluded, is derived from the surface ocean.
From up here. From the lit, warm, busy part of the ocean that we actually touch.

kinetic.sub: 51 ± 14 before 1900 → 81 ± 32 after 1950 · the cores hold the change

scenes.text: The cores hold the change as a timeline. Before nineteen hundred, an average of fifty one nanograms per gram. After nineteen fifty, eighty one.
And the paper is explicit that this rise cannot be explained by a change in how much organic carbon is falling. Something else had to be delivering it.

scenes.chapter:
ACT VI
WHY IT ENDS UP AT THE BOTTOM

scenes.text: So why there? Why would the most remote place on Earth hold more of this than the water above it?
The mechanism people point to is shape. A trench is a funnel with no outlet.

Everything that sinks in the open ocean drifts down slowly and spreads out. Everything that sinks near a trench slides down the walls and collects at the bottom, in a narrow strip, with nowhere further to go.
scenes.cap: A funnel with no outlet.

scenes.text: And at the bottom of that funnel sit the scavengers, eating everything that arrives, concentrating in their own tissue whatever came down with it.

That is the explanation, and it is a good one. But I want to be accurate about its status. It is a mechanism that fits the observations. It is not a proven cause, and the papers themselves do not claim it is.
scenes.cap: A mechanism that fits. Not a proven cause.

scenes.text: There is a lot here that is genuinely unsettled. How fast this is still accumulating. Whether it is harming the animals or simply sitting in them. What the fibres do to an amphipod that has evolved for a diet of whatever falls.
And whether it reaches the snailfish that eat the amphipods. Nobody has published that measurement.
Here is what I think this actually is, and it is not the thing these stories usually get turned into.

The hadal snailfish arrived in the trenches a few million years ago. It gave up its colour, its eyes and the calcium in its bones to be there. It cruises at seven tenths of a body length per second. It can smell a meal from three hundred and fifty metres.
And in the same trench, in every single animal a research team pulled up and opened, there was a blue fibre.
scenes.cap: Every single one.

scenes.text: Sixty five animals out of ninety, across six trenches. It is a small sample and it proves less than a headline wants it to. What it does prove is that there is no longer anywhere on this planet clean enough to use as a control.
scenes.cap: Nowhere left to use as a control.

scenes.text: If the deep ocean holds your attention, there is one animal down there nobody has ever seen alive and intact. Watch Nobody Has Ever Seen a Full-Grown Colossal Squid, right here on mindwired. And subscribe to mindwired, so you don't miss the next case we open from the record.
